newsitem.title: UK: Britain backs N.Irish talks poised for recess.
newsitem.headline: Britain backs N.Irish talks poised for recess.

text.p: Britain pledged support on Tuesday for Northern Ireland peace talks that parties said might be suspended on Wednesday until June.

A spokesman for talks chairman and former U.S. senator George Mitchell told Reuters an adjournment on Wednesday was "possible, but there has been no final decision taken. The decision is up to the parties and the governments."

British and Irish political sources expect the talks, clouded by guerrilla attacks and rising sectarianism in the province, to recess to allow parties to prepare for an election in Britain and Northern Ireland that must be held by late May.

"We believe that this talks process still offers the best opportunity of reaching agreement. It is, as has been said rather overmuch, the only game in town," Northern Ireland Office junior minister Michael Ancram told reporters.
"We want to make sure that it is there and ready to take up its role again once the period of politics...,which we are going to enter fairly shortly, is completed."
Ancram strengthened speculation that Prime Minister John Major will not call a snap election before May.
"We know now the most likely election date is not going to be in March, and probably not going to be in April and you can make your own assumptions after that," Ancram said.
Earlier pro-British Protestant leader Ian Paisley predicted the Anglo-Irish sponsored talks would be suspended on Wednesday.
"What they are going to do (is) they are going to have an axeing operation tomorrow or next Wednesday - and I think it will be tomorrow," Paisley told reporters in Belfast.

Political sources said a May general election contest for the province's 18 parliamentary seats and municipal elections, also scheduled for late May, would make early June a likely date for the talks to be reconvened.

Sinn Fein, the Irish Republican Army's political wing, was excluded from the multi-party talks, held at Stormont Buildings, a government office complex in east Belfast, because the guerrillas refused to call off a war against British rule.
Worried by growing IRA hostilities and a wave of arson attacks on Protestant and Catholic church property, Britain launched a television commercial on Tuesday warning of the dangers of sectarianism.

The 185,000 pound ($299,100) commercial launched by Ancram at a news conference featured infants playing against a soundtrack of new items about violence, and the song "Do You Know Where You're Going To."
Ancram said Britain had decided not to draw a parallel between the province and pre-war Nazi Germany.

Recently British sources said that a commercial, including flashbacks to scenes of Nazi persecution of Jews, was being considered as a way of highlighting sectarian strife which has accelerated over the past year.

"Our view is that there is more impact to be gained by looking at actual things that are happening here at this time, and that comparisons of a historical nature wherever were not the most effective way of making that impact," Ancram said.
Political sources said a second commercial was being made which would have film scenes of Northern Ireland violence intercut. ($1=.6186 Pound)
